prompt: Where does AWS put a CUR 2.0 export?
hint: Nobody reads it for you.

choices.text: In Cost Explorer, as a new report on its screen
choices.why: Cost Explorer draws its screens from the same data, but the export is files, delivered somewhere you query them.

choices.text: As files in an S3 bucket you name
choices.why: Right. Parquet or compressed CSV, under the bucket and prefix the export names, refreshed during the month.

choices.text: Attached to the monthly invoice e-mail
choices.why: The invoice is a summary. The report has a row per line of the bill, far too many for an attachment.

choices.text: In a database AWS runs for the account
choices.why: AWS delivers files; querying them, with Athena or anything else, is a separate choice you make.

prompt: `aws bcm-data-exports create-export --export file://export.json` answers with a 500 in the lab. What does the run still show?
hint: What did the command line do before sending?

choices.text: That the export was created and its first files are on the way
choices.why: A 500 is a failure, and moto has no Data Exports at all; nothing was created.

choices.text: That the field names match AWS's API; the values were not judged
choices.why: Right. A misspelt field is refused with `Unknown parameter` before anything is sent, so the request reached moto.

choices.text: That `PARQUET` is a format AWS accepts for exports
choices.why: That comes from AWS's documentation. Nothing in the lab checked the value.

choices.text: That the bucket `shop-logs` lacks a policy for the billing service
choices.why: The bucket was never consulted: the 500 is moto lacking the whole service.

prompt: Without `INCLUDE_RESOURCES`, which question can the export no longer answer?
hint: Which column does it add?

choices.text: Which account used a line
choices.why: `line_item_usage_account_id` is there either way.

choices.text: Which usage type a line is
choices.why: `line_item_usage_type` does not depend on the option.

choices.text: Which instance or gateway caused a line
choices.why: Right. The option adds `line_item_resource_id`; without it a line says what and where, not which one.

choices.text: What a line cost at its unblended rate
choices.why: Cost is on every line, resource or not.

prompt: Match each CUR 2.0 column to what it holds.
hint: Payer and user are different accounts.

pairs.right: the exact thing, such as NAT gateway hours
the activated tags, as a map

prompt: The shop adds a new tag key, `cost-centre`, and activates it. What changes in a CUR 2.0 table compared with the older report?
hint: One column, or a column per tag?

choices.text: A new column `resource_tags_user_cost_centre` appears, as before
choices.why: That was the older report's shape. CUR 2.0 keeps one map column.

choices.text: Nothing in the table's shape: the key appears inside `resource_tags`
choices.why: Right. The map gains a key on the lines that carry it, and every query written before keeps working.

choices.text: Every earlier line gains the key, back to the start of the year
choices.why: Activation is not retroactive (lesson 13), and the tag must have been on the resource at the time.

choices.text: The export must be deleted and created again to include it
choices.why: Activated tags reach `resource_tags` without editing the export.

prompt: Three teams run containers on one EKS cluster of shared EC2 instances. What does split cost allocation data add to the report?
hint: The instance is one line; the teams are three.

choices.text: A tag on each instance naming the team that used it most
choices.why: Nothing is tagged by the option, and a single owner per instance is what it exists to avoid.

choices.text: A separate bill for each Kubernetes namespace
choices.why: There is still one bill. The option adds columns to the same report.

choices.text: Columns that split each instance's cost
choices.why: Right. The `split_line_item_*` columns divide it by the processor and memory each container reserved or used, so each team gets its share of a shared machine.

choices.text: Nothing: containers are not in the Cost and Usage Report
choices.why: The instances are, as lines; the option is what divides them among containers.

prompt: Where did the costs in `cur.csv` come from?
hint: Read the docstring of `make_cur.py`.

choices.text: From moto, which kept a record of the lab's resources
choices.why: moto bills nothing and has no report; the file was written by a program.

choices.text: Made-up quantities times price-list rates from earlier lessons
choices.why: Right. The rates were read in lessons 1, 13 and 14; the accounts, quantities, credit and tax are invented.

choices.text: From a real export of the shop's management account
choices.why: There is no AWS account behind the course, so there is no export to copy.

choices.text: From AWS's sample report, published with the Data Exports documentation
choices.why: The file is generated by the program in the lesson, line by line.

prompt: In `cur.csv`, `SavingsPlanCoveredUsage` is 117.27 and `SavingsPlanNegation` is -117.27. What do the plan's three lines add up to, in dollars?
hint: The two usage lines cancel; one line is left.

prompt: Somebody totals only the lines of type `Usage` and reports 673.59 as the month. What is missing from that number?
hint: Read the second query's table.

choices.text: Nothing; `Usage` is every charge
choices.why: It is one type among six in the file; the plan, tax and credit are other types.

choices.text: Only the tax, which is added at the end of the month
choices.why: Tax is missing, and so are the plan's fee and the sandbox's credit.

choices.text: The plan's fee, the tax and the credit
choices.why: Right. Each is a line type of its own. All types together are the 806.60 the first query printed.

choices.text: The instance covered by the plan, which `Usage` leaves out on purpose
choices.why: Its covered usage and negation cancel anyway; what is missing is the fee that paid for it, plus tax and credit.

prompt: `ask.py` needs nothing installed because Python's own library carries ___, a whole SQL database in one module.
hint: Its name is in the import.

prompt: `ask.py` declares three columns `REAL` and every other column `TEXT`. What would go wrong if the money columns were text?
hint: Think about sorting by the result.

choices.text: `sum` would refuse to run on them
choices.why: SQLite converts text that looks like a number when it adds; the sum would run.

choices.text: `9.5` would sort after `117.27`
choices.why: Right. Values stored as text compare character by character. Declaring the column `REAL` keeps every comparison numeric.

choices.text: The CSV would fail to load
choices.why: Text loads anything; that is why it would load and then compare wrongly.

choices.text: Negative costs would lose their minus sign
choices.why: The sign is kept as a character in text, and as a sign in a number.

prompt: Unblended, the web team's month is 376.55; amortised, 456.23. Where were the other 79.68 in the unblended view?
hint: Which line carries no tag?

choices.text: In the data team, which uses the same instance type
choices.why: The data team is 165.90 in both columns; nothing moved there.

choices.text: In `(no team)`, on the plan's fee line, which has no tags
choices.why: Right. Amortised moves the fee onto the covered line, which is tagged `web`, and the remainder drops by the same 79.68.

choices.text: In the tax, which the query left out
choices.why: Tax is excluded from both columns alike, so it cannot explain a difference between them.

choices.text: Nowhere; amortised adds a charge AWS never made
choices.why: The 79.68 was charged, as the plan's fee. Amortised only says whose it was.

prompt: The finance team asks two questions: what did we pay AWS this month, and what did each team's usage cost. Which column answers which?
hint: One is about the invoice; one is about the hours.

choices.text: Amortised for both, because it is the honest one
choices.why: Honest for teams. A prepaid year shows as a twelfth a month amortised, which is not what was paid that month.

choices.text: Unblended for both, because it is what AWS charged
choices.why: Per team it charges a shared commitment to nobody, and the team that used it looks free.

choices.text: Amortised for the invoice, unblended for the teams
choices.why: That is the pairing reversed: it would spread payments across months and leave the plan's fee untagged.

choices.text: Unblended for the invoice, amortised for the teams
choices.why: Right. Unblended is what was charged; amortised charges a commitment to the usage it covered.

prompt: Staging's usage is 227.06 dollars, of which 93.79 carries no `team` tag. What percentage is untagged, to the nearest whole number?
hint: Untagged divided by usage, times 100.

prompt: Which of these must a showback or chargeback scheme decide by a written rule, because no tag will settle them? Choose all that apply.
hint: The section names three.

choices.text: Who owns the untagged remainder
choices.why: Right. The account's owner, or a split in proportion to what the teams claimed.

choices.text: How tax and support are split
choices.why: Right. They are shared lines, usually split in proportion to usage.

choices.text: Which account an instance's hours belong to
choices.why: That is a column, `line_item_usage_account_id`, on every line; it needs no rule.

choices.text: Whether commitments are charged amortised to the usage they covered
choices.why: Right. Otherwise the team that bought the plan for everybody looks expensive.

choices.text: Which usage type a NAT gateway's hours are
choices.why: AWS writes the usage type on the line; it is not the shop's to decide.

prompt: What is the difference between showback and chargeback?
hint: One moves money; one does not.

choices.text: Showback reports each team's cost; chargeback moves it into the team's budget
choices.why: Right. Both need the same rules; chargeback makes every rule matter more, because money follows them.

choices.text: Showback uses unblended cost; chargeback uses amortised
choices.why: Either can use either column. The difference is what happens to the number, not how it is counted.

choices.text: Showback is Cost Explorer; chargeback is the Cost and Usage Report
choices.why: They are ways of using the answer, not tools for getting it.

choices.text: Showback covers only tagged costs; chargeback covers the remainder
choices.why: Both have to account for the untagged remainder, by a rule.

prompt: At the size of a real organisation, which pair is the AWS way to query the report and draw it?
hint: One runs SQL over S3; one draws dashboards.

choices.text: Cost Explorer and Budgets
choices.why: They read the same data through fixed screens; neither queries the report's files.

choices.text: Athena and QuickSight
choices.why: Right. Athena runs SQL directly over the Parquet in S3; QuickSight draws dashboards from its answers. Neither was run here.

choices.text: sqlite3 and `ask.py`, copied into the bucket
choices.why: They are the lab's stand-ins on your own machine, not something AWS runs.

choices.text: Cost Anomaly Detection and SNS
choices.why: They watch patterns and send alerts; they do not query the report.

prompt: Put in order what has to exist before a report can split September's costs by `team`.
hint: The tag first, then billing, then the files, then the question.
items: resources carry `team` while they run in September
the key `team` is activated in the management account
the export writes September's lines to the bucket
trap: Putting the activation before the tags is also possible in practice, but the key only appears in Billing once something carries it; the tag on the resource during the month is what nothing afterwards can supply.

prompt: A real report shows 30% of production's usage untagged, mostly `SAE1-PublicIPv4:InUseAddress` and `USE1-APIRequest`. What is the first, cheapest step?
hint: Some lines can be claimed by a rule faster than by tags.

choices.text: Delete every resource without a `team` tag
choices.why: The addresses are in use by something running; deleting what is unowned is not the same as deleting what is unused.

choices.text: Switch the report from unblended to amortised
choices.why: Amortised moves commitments; these lines are on demand and would stay untagged.

choices.text: Read them by usage type, then tag or assign each by rule
choices.why: Right. Every untagged line names what it is; the remainder is unowned, not unknown, and the rule says whose it becomes.

choices.text: Request a backfill so the tags apply to the past twelve months
choices.why: A backfill applies an activation, not a tag the resources never carried.

prompt: A query groups by `line_item_usage_account_id` and another by `bill_payer_account_id`. On a consolidated bill, what does the second one print?
hint: Lesson 3: who receives the bill?

choices.text: The same three accounts as the first
choices.why: The member accounts use; they do not pay. Only the first query splits by them.

choices.text: One row: the management account, with the whole bill
choices.why: Right. In `cur.csv` every line's payer is `123456789012`, as on a real consolidated bill.

choices.text: An error, because the column is empty for member accounts
choices.why: The column is filled on every line; for a member account it names the payer.

choices.text: Each team, since teams are what pay
choices.why: Teams are tags. The payer is an account.
